mem.t: Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says the LORD of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there will not be enough room for.

lessons.title: Everything Belongs to God
lessons.theme: I am not an owner but a steward of God’s resources

v: The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.

lessons.still: Look at the things around you: your phone, your wallet, the table and chairs, your clothes. One by one, say to the Lord, “This is yours.” Finally, place your hand on your chest and quietly say, “And I am yours too.”
teach: A hotel guest may use everything in the room: the bed, the lamps, the towels, the air conditioning. Yet no one thinks the towels belong to them; at checkout everything is handed back as it was. So it is with us in this world: nothing we use is truly ours. It has all been entrusted to us for a while.

Psalm 24:1 declares that the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord. When David gave toward building the temple, the people gladly offered great amounts of gold and silver, yet David said, “Who am I … we have given you of your own.” Giving is not handing God something of ours; it is giving back to God what is his. The real question is not “How much should I give to God?” but “How much should I keep for myself?”

Once our mindset changes, money weighs differently: from “my money” to “the Lord’s money,” from “what I earned” to “what he gave,” from the temporary to the eternal. Money is the most honest test of who is reigning. We can sing “The Lord is my King” at church, but our bank statements tell the truth.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus reign must include our wallets. The self-ruled life says, “This is mine”; the self-emptied life says, “This is the Lord’s.” Pride is grasping power, and money is the easiest power to grasp. Handing ownership back to God is returning to our place as stewards.
q: Who is God? — “All things come from you.” What does this show you about God?
Who am I? — Right now, do you relate to money more like an owner or a steward?
How shall I respond? — Over which possession will you concretely hand ownership back to the Lord?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Caesar’s image was on the coin, but God’s image is on us. God wants not only our money but our whole selves, the people who bear his image.
lessons.pray: Lord, the earth and everything in it are yours, and I am yours too. I confess that I often treat what you have entrusted to me as my own property. Today I hand ownership back to you. Be Lord of my wallet, and make me a faithful steward. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write “This is the Lord’s” on or beside your wallet or payment app
Review last month’s spending and see where the money went
Pray over one possession you have been clinging to, and entrust it to God
lessons.noon: “And we have given you of your own.” — Lord, right now all that I have is yours.

lessons.title: The Tithe
lessons.theme: Tithing is a lesson in faith, not a transaction to buy blessing

v: Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says the LORD of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there will not be enough room for.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith. But you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone.

lessons.still: Quietly ask yourself, “Do I really believe God will provide for me?” There is no need to rush an answer. Let the Holy Spirit shine on your fears and your sources of security where money is concerned, and lay them openly before the Lord.
teach: A farmer keeps back his best bag of seed to sow in the field rather than grinding it into flour. Others see one less bag of grain; the farmer sees faith in the coming harvest. The tithe is like that: not a loss, but faith sown into God’s storehouse.

In Malachi’s day the people were robbing God of the tithe they owed, yet God invited them: “Test me now in this.” It is one of the rare places in Scripture where God himself invites people to put him to the test. Jesus also said tithing should “not be left undone,” yet he rebuked the Pharisees even more for neglecting “justice, mercy, and faith.” The tithe is not the finishing line but the starting line; not a legal calculation but an expression of love and trust.

Beware of two errors. One treats the tithe as an investment to buy blessing: “I give God ten, so God owes me a hundred.” That is prosperity theology. The other uses grace as an excuse to give nothing at all. Grace comes first: we do not give to earn blessing; we give because we have already been blessed. The tithe is a concrete practice of “letting God be God” with our money.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Of the eight steps for changing our mindset, Practice and Review are nowhere more visible than with money. Tithing is a practical act of letting Jesus reign, and it also supplies what builds God’s kingdom system, so that there is food in God’s house and the work of the kingdom can move forward.
q: Who is God? — God says, “Test me now in this.” What does this show you about his faithfulness?
Who am I? — In giving, are you more prone to the error of “buying blessing” or of “not giving”?
How shall I respond? — What step of faith are you willing to take in your giving?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never avoided talking about money, but he always saw the heart behind it. When Zacchaeus gave half his possessions to the poor, Jesus said, “Today, salvation has come to this house.” The turning of his money bore witness to the turning of his heart.
lessons.pray: Faithful Father, you say, “Test me now in this,” and I want to answer you in faith. Take away my fear of not having enough, and take away any desire to trade my giving for blessing. I give because I have already been blessed; I offer because you are my King. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Honestly work out what proportion of your income you currently give
Before you next give, pray first and set the amount in faith
As you give, pray silently, “Lord, I give because I have already been blessed.”
lessons.noon: “And test me now in this,” says the LORD of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven” — Lord, right now I trust in your provision.

lessons.title: The Widow’s Two Small Coins
lessons.theme: God looks not at the amount but at the heart and the cost

v: Jesus sat down opposite the treasury and saw how the multitude cast money into the treasury. Many who were rich cast in much.
A poor widow came and she cast in two small brass coins, which equal a quadrans coin.
He called his disciples to himself and said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury,
for they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.”

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus sitting opposite the treasury, watching you. His gaze is not one of judgement but of tenderness. Quietly say to the Lord, “Lord, you see what I offer, and you see my heart.”
teach: A child spends their pocket money on a single flower for their mother. It wilts in a few days and cost very little, yet the mother presses it in a book and treasures it for years, because that flower carries the child’s whole heart. In love, value is never measured by the price tag.

Jesus “sat down opposite the treasury, and saw how the multitude cast money” in. He was watching how, not just how much. The rich put in large amounts; the widow put in only two small coins. Yet Jesus’ verdict turns everything upside down: “This poor widow gave more than all those who are giving.” For the rich gave out of their abundance, but she gave out of her poverty, all she had to live on.

God does not measure how much you give but how much you keep, and what it costs you. This comforts the poor: a small gift is not small in God’s eyes. It also challenges the well-off: a large sum is not necessarily a large offering. The widow entrusted her whole self to God; her two small coins were an act of total trust in him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The widow’s gift was a self-emptied gift: not given to be seen, with no fallback, relying wholly on God. Her focus was on God, not on what others thought. A shift in perspective: from human eyes to God’s eyes, from the outward amount to the inward heart.
q: Who is God? — Jesus “sat down opposite the treasury” and watched closely. What does this show you about him?
Who am I? — Do you mostly give out of “abundance,” or have you ever given out of “poverty”?
How shall I respond? — What “two small coins” could you offer wholeheartedly to the Lord today?
lessons.jesus: Not long after speaking about the widow, Jesus himself gave everything, not just what he had to live on but his very life. The widow put in two small coins; Jesus put in himself. He is the most complete giver of all.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for seeing the offerings no one notices. I will no longer compare amounts; I only want to give you my true heart. Teach me the widow’s trust and your own self-giving, so that I place all I have in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Make an offering that costs you something, whatever the amount
Quietly help a brother or sister in financial difficulty, without letting anyone know
Thank God for someone you know who gives sacrificially without being noticed
lessons.noon: “This poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury” — Lord, right now I offer you my true heart.

lessons.title: A Cheerful Giver

v: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.
Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.

lessons.still: Remember the joy you felt when you gave a gift to someone you love. Bring that feeling before the Lord and quietly say, “Lord, may I feel that same joy when I give to you and to others.”
teach: A fountain stays fresh because water keeps flowing in and keeps flowing out. The Dead Sea is dead because water only flows in and never out. If money only ever comes in and never goes out, the heart slowly grows heavy and dry. Cheerful giving keeps life flowing.

The churches of Macedonia, in deep poverty, overflowed in rich generosity. Paul points to the source: the Lord Jesus was rich, yet for our sake he became poor. The motivation for giving is not command but grace. So Paul says, “not grudgingly or under compulsion,” because “God loves a cheerful giver.” God looks not only at what we give but at how we give.

“He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” is not a formula for return on investment but a spiritual principle: generous people experience more of God’s grace, so that they have “all sufficiency in everything” and “abound to every good work.” God gives to us so that we can give again. A shift in mindset: from “protecting what’s mine” to “circulating what is God’s.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. Cheerful giving is an act of thankful worship. The final step on the path of service is “God”: giving glory to God and giving thanks in everything. Reluctant giving is the calculation of the self-ruled life; cheerful giving is the overflow of the self-emptied life.
q: Who is God? — “Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor.” What does this show you about Christ?
Who am I? — Is your giving mostly cheerful, or grudging and under compulsion?
How shall I respond? — How could you cheerfully bless someone this week?
lessons.jesus: Paul quotes the Lord Jesus: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” This sums up Jesus’ whole life: he gave healing, he gave his time, he gave forgiveness, and in the end he gave his life. His giving was never forced, for he gave willingly and gladly.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you were rich, yet for my sake you became poor, and your grace has made me rich. Put a cheerful heart within me, so that I give neither grudgingly nor under compulsion. Like a fountain, let your grace flow out through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Plan one act of cheerful giving this week, and pray over it with joy
Buy a brother or sister a coffee and sincerely ask how they are doing
Write down three ways the Lord has made you “rich”
lessons.noon: “God loves a cheerful giver” — Lord, right now let your grace flow out through me.

lessons.title: Treasure in Heaven
lessons.theme: Store up treasure in heaven, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be

v: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal;
but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal;
for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
Charge those who are rich in this present age that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy;

lessons.still: Imagine yourself standing at the end of your life, looking back. Which things will be left behind on earth? Which will be carried into eternity? Be still for a while, and let the Lord rearrange the order of values in your heart.
teach: People emigrating to another country do not leave all their assets in the place they are leaving; they transfer their resources to the country where they are going. We are citizens of heaven, and earth is only where we are staying for a while. We cannot take our earthly wealth with us, but we can “transfer” our treasure to heaven ahead of time.

Jesus names three dangers for earthly treasure: moth, rust and thieves, natural decay and human theft. Treasure in heaven, however, is never lost. Verse 21 gets to the heart of it: where your treasure is, there your heart will be. Money not only reveals the direction of the heart; it pulls the heart in that direction. Paul likewise charges the rich not to put their hope in uncertain riches but in God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.

This week we have moved from everything belongs to God (Day 1), the tithe (Day 2), the widow’s heart (Day 3) and the cheerful giver (Day 4) to today’s treasure in heaven. Investing money in people’s eternal lives is storing up treasure in heaven. Next week we will see another precious treasure of God’s kingdom: the unity of brothers and sisters.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift in perspective: from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Using money to build people up, to equip them and to share the gospel is transferring treasure to heaven and building God’s kingdom system.
q: Who is God? — God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy.” What does this show you about him?
Who am I? — Looking at your spending, where is your heart right now?
How shall I respond? — This week, which of your resources could you invest in someone’s eternal life?
lessons.jesus: Jesus stored up no treasure on earth; he said, “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” Yet he was the richest of all, because his treasure was the Father’s delight and the souls of people. He gave up everything to redeem us; we are his treasure.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, take away my heart’s reliance on money. Everything on earth will pass away; only you and your kingdom remain for ever. Teach me to store up treasure in heaven and to invest my resources in people’s lives, so that my heart follows hard after you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Set aside an amount in this month’s budget specifically for evangelism or care
Sort out something you no longer need and give it to someone who needs it
Share with your family or a spiritual companion: “Where is my treasure?”
lessons.noon: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” — Lord, right now my heart is with you.
